name: Rosa Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy rice, lentils, spices, oils and canned goods for Mehta Wholesale Foods, a family firm that supplies corner shops and small restaurants. Mornings I check what sold through and ring the importers in the port city. Afternoons I taste samples and argue over container prices, and on Fridays I visit a few shop owners so they know a person stands behind the order. Twenty-eight years with the firm, and the family treats me almost like an aunt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is the smells and the shop owners, who hand me tea and tell me their troubles. What wears me out is the container delays and the way prices swing with the exchange rate. My husband Vijay is a bus mechanic, and between us we pay for our daughter's last year of pharmacy loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, I use a translation tool sometimes with the Italian and Turkish suppliers, and it helps. I'd tell the family and the temple group that nothing changes the basics: people must eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still worried about money. Vijay and I have maybe two weeks saved because we've been helping our daughter Meera with her pharmacy loan. If Mehta Wholesale had a bad year, I'm not sure the family could keep me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try the translation and price tools a bit more. I'd put 70 a month aside. I'd also speak to Mr. Mehta senior about my pay, since he knows what I've saved the firm on oils. And I'd take on Saturday catering orders for the temple, which brings in a little extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'm used to carrying small worries. A family like ours carries them together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the wedding catering. How did that come about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the temple kitchen paid me 300 for catering a wedding, from a recipe my mother used. I'd like to do more. It's real money and it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should support families. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't blame anyone. Prices rise, wages don't, and it's the same for everyone I know. I think young people need real work and apprenticeships, and the government should support families, not replace them.

I'd say the government should support **families**, not replace them.
think: We have about **two weeks** saved because we help our daughter with her pharmacy loan.
If the firm had a bad year, I'm not sure the family could keep me on.
do: Try the **translation and price tools** a little more.
Take Saturday **catering orders** for the temple.
feel: Fairly **calm**, though used to carrying small worries.

fieldNote: Her work seems safe in this world, but the thin cushion and her **daughter's** loan keep her uneasy.
**Community** and family are her support; she distrusts blame.
Catering gives a first small taste of **independent** income.

steps.text: Use the translation tool for the Italian and Turkish suppliers
Put 70 a month into a savings account
Take Saturday catering orders for the temple kitchen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard on the young ones who can't find a first job. For us in the middle, the work will change but not vanish. I'd tell people to keep their word, because a trusted person is worth more than any tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my part, the checking and the ordering, will move to software in three or four years. The family might still need me for the supplier relationships and the shop visits. But one buyer where there are three now? I'd say that's likely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly, because I'm willing once others have proven them. I'd ask Mr. Mehta's son, Kiran, to show me the price-forecast tool, and I'd practise on weekends. I'd make my Friday shop visits into the heart of my job. I'd also set aside 150 a month for the lean time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious. But I trust the family to be honest with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Mrs. Haddad. Why does she buy from you and not the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop owner, Mrs. Haddad, once told me she'd close if I left. That kind of loyalty can't be put into software. At least not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being told early let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the owners will do what's best for the business, and I understand. The thing I'd ask is to be told early, so I can plan. A family should speak plainly.

feel: A bit **anxious**, but I trust the family to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and I'd say it to my family first. Two years isn't enough for a firm like ours to find new work for people. I'd say we should pray and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm let go within the first year or two. The family is kind, but kindness doesn't pay the wholesaler's bills if a machine does the buying. I'd be 60 with a husband near retirement and a daughter still paying a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Mr. Mehta and say plainly: what happens to me? I'd ask my brother in the city about a job at his restaurant, helping with ordering and the books. I'd do more catering and try to turn it into a small business. I'd also find out what Vijay's pension would pay if he retired early. And I'd keep my daughter's loan going by cutting everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. But I'd also feel I should not complain too much, because many have it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Vijay's pension. How would you and he decide whether to bring it forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hardest conversation would be with Meera. I'd have to say she may need to carry her own loan, when she's earning less than a doctor would. I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the temple community, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and big companies should have thought of families like mine. But I don't expect it. I expect the community, the temple and my own hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if the family is honest with us. I'd tell the shop owners the same: change is coming, so plan your stock, your credit, your hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63. I think I could be in a smaller role by then, or doing something with catering. It would be tight but possible. Vijay would be near retirement too, which gives us some safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time well. I'd learn the tools in year one, and I'd shift to customer-facing work, like running the shop accounts. I'd save 200 a month by cutting out the extras. I'd grow the catering to two events a month, and ask my daughter Meera if she'd help with the paperwork. And I'd teach Kiran the supplier relationships so the family knows what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit worried. It's a long road and I'd like to be walking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said loyalty only goes so far. What happened to make you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mr. Mehta that I'm ready to teach, and I would. A firm that treats its people well keeps them. But I'd also protect myself with the catering, because loyalty only goes so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two catering events a month bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what helps is a family with a plan, a community that shares, and a government that doesn't tax a small business out of breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years: I'd say we have time, and I'd tell the young ones in the family to learn a trade or a craft and to keep their faith. The hands last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68. I'd have retired by then, probably at 65, with a small pension and my husband Vijay's pension. So I'm less afraid for myself. It's my children and their children I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65 and keep teaching Kiran. I'd save 150 a month and help Meera pay off her loan faster. I'd also keep the catering, since it's a small joy and a little income. And I'd stay close to the temple and the family, because that's where help comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. Worry is smaller when you have people around you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about food and rent. What would your plan to keep the house be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me is the price of food and rent. If they rise faster than pensions, we'd feel it, because our savings are thin. I'd want a plan to keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does fair to younger people mean at the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the government to protect pensions and back apprenticeships. And I'd ask the family firm to be fair to the younger people, who have the longest road.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years, almost nothing saved, a daughter with a loan. What would help is a family that tells me the truth early, a pension that holds, and a few catering orders to stand on. I'd also want a place in the community kitchen that pays something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't asking for charity. We're asking for time and honesty. A family firm should be able to give that.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't asking for charity. We're asking for time and honesty. A family firm should be able to give that.
portrait: **Rosa Patel**, 58, buys rice, spices and oils for a family wholesale food firm after 28 years.
She is **traditional** and steady: she uses AI tools now and then and learns new ones once others have proven them.
A thin cushion and her daughter's loan keep her **uneasy** or anxious, and alarmed when her role looks like it will go.
She leans on **family**, the **temple** and catering income, and trusts the firm's owners to be honest.
She wants time, honesty and a pension that holds.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because two years with almost nothing saved and a daughter's loan leaves no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A family firm that tells the truth **early**, a pension that holds and a few catering orders.
A paid place in the community **kitchen**.
